target_text: Egbe bere ugo bere nke si ibe ya ebela nku kwaa ya
english_translation: Live and let live; anyone denying others freedom deserves the consequences.
literal_translation: Let the kite perch, let the eagle perch; whichever tells the other not to perch, let its wing break.
cultural_note: The best known of all Igbo proverbs and often treated as a statement of the Igbo social contract. The kite and the eagle are both birds of prey with equal claim to the sky, so the image argues for coexistence between equals rather than tolerance granted by a superior to an inferior. It is invoked in disputes over land, office and communal rights.

target_text: Onye kwe chi ya ekwe
english_translation: When someone is determined their personal destiny supports them.
literal_translation: If a person agrees, his chi agrees.
cultural_note: Rests on the concept of chi, the personal spirit or destiny that accompanies each individual. The proverb places human will first: the chi responds to the person's own consent rather than dictating to them, which is why Igbo thought is often described as balancing destiny with personal effort.

target_text: Igwe bụ ike
english_translation: Unity is strength.
literal_translation: Multitude is strength.
cultural_note: A short, widely used motto found on town union banners, age-grade associations and family crests. It underpins the communal decision-making tradition in which authority rests with the assembly rather than a single ruler.

target_text: Otu osisi anaghị eme ọhịa
english_translation: One tree cannot make a forest; cooperation is necessary.
literal_translation: One tree does not make a forest.
cultural_note: Used to check individualism, especially when someone claims sole credit for communal achievement. Often paired in speech with the one-hand proverb below.

target_text: Otu aka anaghị ebu ngwugwu
english_translation: One hand cannot lift a heavy load; people need help.
literal_translation: One hand does not carry a bundle.
cultural_note: A practical companion to the forest proverb. Commonly cited when asking for assistance without shame, since needing help is framed as ordinary rather than weak.

target_text: Onye nwere mmadụ ka onye nwere ego
english_translation: Having supportive people is greater than having money.
literal_translation: One who has people surpasses one who has money.
cultural_note: Expresses the ranking of social capital above material wealth. It is often quoted at funerals and title ceremonies, where the size and warmth of the gathering is read as the true measure of a life.

target_text: Nwanne dị na mba
english_translation: Your relative or helper may be found anywhere.
literal_translation: A sibling exists in foreign lands.
cultural_note: A diaspora proverb long before the modern diaspora. It legitimises kinship formed through kindness rather than blood and is the traditional greeting logic behind Igbo town unions abroad.

target_text: Agwọ nọ n'akịrịka bụ akịrịka chebere ya
english_translation: A person is often protected by their environment or community.
literal_translation: The snake in the thicket is protected by the thicket.
cultural_note: A caution against despising the community that shields you. It is also used in reverse, to warn that someone's apparent power may belong to their backers rather than themselves.

target_text: A na-amata dike n'agha
english_translation: A brave person is known during difficult times.
literal_translation: A warrior is known in battle.
cultural_note: Dike is not merely a fighter but a person of proven capacity. The proverb withholds judgement until pressure arrives, and is often used to defer praise rather than to give it.

target_text: Ihe onye metara ọ buru
english_translation: Everyone must face the consequences of their actions.
literal_translation: What one has done, one carries.
cultural_note: A statement of personal accountability that limits how far kin are expected to absorb an individual's wrongdoing.

target_text: Onye ajụrụ anaghị ajụ onwe ya
english_translation: Rejection should not make you reject or undervalue yourself.
literal_translation: One who is rejected does not reject himself.
cultural_note: Offered as consolation to someone passed over for marriage, office or inclusion. It separates other people's verdict from a person's own estimation of their worth.

target_text: Anụ gbaa ajọ ọsọ a gbaa ya ajọ egbe
english_translation: An extraordinary problem requires an extraordinary response.
literal_translation: If an animal runs an unusual race, it is shot with an unusual gun.
cultural_note: A proportionality proverb from the hunting register. It justifies a severe response as fitted to a severe provocation, and is often used in council to defend an unusual decision.

target_text: Ebe onye dara ka ọ na-ele ọ bụghị ebe ọ sụrụ ngọngọ
english_translation: People often focus on their failure instead of its true cause.
literal_translation: Where a person fell is where he looks, not where he stumbled.
cultural_note: A diagnostic proverb. It argues that the visible collapse is rarely the origin of the problem, and is used to push an inquiry backwards toward the real cause.

target_text: A naghị anọ otu ebe ekiri mmanwụ
english_translation: Look at an issue from different perspectives.
literal_translation: One does not stand in one place to watch a masquerade.
cultural_note: Drawn from the masquerade performance, which moves through the arena so that no single vantage point shows the whole. It is the standard Igbo argument for hearing more than one account before judging.

target_text: Mmanwụ anaghị ama onye nwe ya
english_translation: Power or danger may eventually harm even its creator.
literal_translation: The masquerade does not spare the one who owns it.
cultural_note: A warning against summoning forces you assume will remain loyal. Frequently applied to political violence, thugs and unchecked authority.

target_text: Ezi aha ka ego
english_translation: A good name is more valuable than money.
literal_translation: A good name surpasses money.
cultural_note: Reputation is treated as an inheritable asset in Igbo society, attaching to a family and lineage rather than only an individual.

target_text: Aha ọma ka akụ
english_translation: A good reputation is better than wealth.
literal_translation: A good name surpasses wealth.
cultural_note: A close variant of the preceding proverb, using akụ, accumulated wealth or property, rather than ego, money. The pairing of the two is common in speeches.

target_text: Ọ bụ onye kpọrọ nkụ ka mmiri na-agụ
english_translation: The person experiencing a problem understands it best.
literal_translation: It is the one who gathered the firewood that the rain concerns.
cultural_note: Asserts the authority of lived experience over outside commentary. Often used to hand the floor back to the person actually affected by a decision.

target_text: Afọ anaghị anụ okwu
english_translation: A hungry stomach does not listen to advice.
literal_translation: The stomach does not hear words.
cultural_note: A realist proverb about material need preceding moral instruction. It is used to argue that welfare must come before lecturing.

target_text: Agụụ adịghị ama onye eze
english_translation: Hunger respects neither kings nor ordinary people.
literal_translation: Hunger does not know a king.
cultural_note: A levelling proverb. Hunger is one of several forces in Igbo speech, alongside death and truth, treated as indifferent to rank.

target_text: A na-amụta amụta amaghị amaghị
english_translation: Learning never ends; nobody knows everything.
literal_translation: One keeps learning; not knowing is not knowing.
cultural_note: A humility formula often used by elders when conceding a point to a younger person, and a natural closing proverb for a lesson.

target_text: Aka aja aja na-ebute ọnụ mmanụ mmanụ
english_translation: Hard work brings prosperity and enjoyment.
literal_translation: Hands covered in sand bring a mouth covered in oil.
cultural_note: Built on the farming image of soil on the hands and palm oil on the lips. It dignifies manual labour by tying it directly to the enjoyment that follows.

target_text: Nkịta nwere ndidi na-eri ọkpụkpụ buru ibu
english_translation: Patience brings great rewards.
literal_translation: A dog that has patience eats the big bone.
cultural_note: Ndidi, endurance, is treated as an active virtue rather than passive waiting. The proverb is common counsel to the young and impatient.

target_text: Ihe dị mma na-ewe oge
english_translation: Good things take time.
literal_translation: A good thing takes time.
cultural_note: Used to defend a slow, careful process against pressure for quick results.

target_text: E jiri ụtụtụ mara ụbọchị ọma
english_translation: A good beginning often suggests a good outcome.
literal_translation: One knows a good day by its morning.
cultural_note: Used to praise a promising start, and in its negative form to raise early warning about a venture that begins badly.

target_text: Ụtụtụ tutụ bụ anya ji ahụ ụzọ
english_translation: Starting early helps one succeed.
literal_translation: Early morning is the eye by which one sees the road.
cultural_note: Tied to farming life, where the productive hours are before the heat. It is standard encouragement to begin work early.

target_text: A naghị eji ọsọ agbata ije ọma
english_translation: Important work should not be rushed.
literal_translation: One does not run in order to make a good journey.
cultural_note: Distinguishes speed from progress. Frequently used to slow down a decision that people want made hastily.

target_text: Ngana kpuchie ute agụụ ekpughee ya
english_translation: Hunger eventually exposes a lazy person.
literal_translation: Laziness covers itself with a mat; hunger uncovers it.
cultural_note: A sharp proverb about consequences arriving on their own schedule. The mat image suggests laziness disguised as rest.

target_text: Onye ụra na-atọ ụgwọ ji ya
english_translation: Too much comfort or laziness can leave obligations unpaid.
literal_translation: He who finds sleep sweet is held by debt.
cultural_note: Pairs comfort with accumulating obligation. Often used where someone enjoys the present while a duty goes unmet.

target_text: Onye rụọ o rie
english_translation: Those who work deserve to eat.
literal_translation: Whoever works, let him eat.
cultural_note: A statement of earned entitlement that also functions as a defence of the worker's claim on the product of their labour.

target_text: Onye anaghị arụ ọrụ ya atụla anya iri
english_translation: Do not expect rewards without effort.
literal_translation: One who does not work should not expect to eat.
cultural_note: The negative form of the preceding proverb. The two are often quoted together as a pair.

target_text: Onye buru chi ya ụzọ ọ gbagbuo onwe ya n'ọsọ
english_translation: Do not try to run ahead of your destiny.
literal_translation: One who goes ahead of his chi kills himself running.
cultural_note: The counterweight to onye kwe chi ya ekwe. Together the two proverbs frame the Igbo view of effort and destiny as partners, where either one running ahead of the other is a failure.

target_text: Onye na-amaghị ebe mmiri bidoro mawa ya agaghị ama ebe ọ kwụsịrị
english_translation: To understand the present you must know the past.
literal_translation: One who does not know where the rain began to beat him will not know where it stopped.
cultural_note: A history proverb, quoted often in discussions of origins, migration and unresolved grievance. It treats ignorance of the past as an obstacle to any real resolution.

target_text: Ọkụkọ ruo n'ụlọ mmadụ ọ mara ebe ọ ga-anọ
english_translation: In another person's home behave respectfully.
literal_translation: When a fowl enters someone's house, it knows where to stand.
cultural_note: Governs conduct as a guest. Even the fowl, the least ceremonious of animals, is credited with knowing its place in another compound.

target_text: Ọkụkọ anaghị echefu onye fụrụ ya ọdụ n'ụbọchị mmiri
english_translation: Never forget someone who helped you during hardship.
literal_translation: A fowl does not forget the one who dried its tail on a rainy day.
cultural_note: Gratitude for help given in bad weather is a recurring theme in Igbo speech. The proverb is used both to praise loyalty and to shame those who forget benefactors.

target_text: A naghị agba aka ahụ nne mmadụ
english_translation: Never visit someone empty-handed when a gift is appropriate.
literal_translation: One does not go empty-handed to see someone's mother.
cultural_note: Codifies the expectation that a visit carries something with it. The gift is a token of regard rather than payment, and its absence reads as indifference.

target_text: Onye wetara oji wetara ndụ
english_translation: Offering kola nuts represents welcome peace and goodwill.
literal_translation: He who brings kola brings life.
cultural_note: Kola nut, oji, opens nearly every formal Igbo gathering. Its breaking and sharing is a rite of welcome, prayer and peace, and this proverb is spoken as part of that rite.

target_text: Oji anaghị aghọta Bekee
english_translation: Traditional customs should be observed in their proper cultural form.
literal_translation: Kola does not understand English.
cultural_note: Said when the kola rite is about to be performed, marking the switch into Igbo. It asserts that certain ceremonies lose their meaning if conducted in a borrowed language.

target_text: Ọnụ kwuru njọ ga-ekwu mma
english_translation: A person who speaks badly can also choose to speak well.
literal_translation: The mouth that spoke evil will speak good.
cultural_note: Holds open the possibility of repair after harsh words. It is used in reconciliation, particularly to allow an offender a route back.

target_text: Ọnụ anaghị agba ọsọ karịa onye nwe ya
english_translation: Think before speaking because you are responsible for your words.
literal_translation: The mouth does not run faster than its owner.
cultural_note: Ties speech firmly to the speaker. A person cannot disown what their mouth has committed them to.

target_text: Ire dị nro na-agbaji ọkpụkpụ
english_translation: Gentle words can overcome strong resistance.
literal_translation: A soft tongue breaks bone.
cultural_note: A negotiation proverb, valuing persuasion over force. It is often quoted before sending an emissary into a difficult conversation.

target_text: Eziokwu bụ ndụ
english_translation: Truth gives life and preserves trust.
literal_translation: Truth is life.
cultural_note: One of the shortest and most frequently invoked Igbo proverbs, used in oath-taking and in settling disputes.

target_text: Ụgha nwere obere ụkwụ
english_translation: Lies do not travel far before they are discovered.
literal_translation: A lie has short legs.
cultural_note: The natural counterpart to eziokwu bụ ndụ. The two are commonly spoken in sequence.

target_text: Ihe e dere ede anaghị efu
english_translation: Written information is preserved better than memory alone.
literal_translation: What is written down is not lost.
cultural_note: A comparatively modern proverb reflecting the value placed on literacy and record-keeping, and often quoted in support of formal education.

target_text: Nwata kwọọ aka ọ soro okenye rie nri
english_translation: A well-behaved child earns respect among elders.
literal_translation: If a child washes his hands, he eats with elders.
cultural_note: Access to the elders' company is presented as earned through conduct rather than granted by age. Widely used in raising children and in praising a young person's maturity.

target_text: A na-esi n'ụlọ mara mma pụta ama
english_translation: Good character and success begin at home.
literal_translation: One looks good from inside the house before coming out to the square.
cultural_note: Locates responsibility for a person's public conduct in their upbringing. Frequently cited in discussions of parenting.

target_text: Nne bụ nne ma nwa bụrụ ajọ nwa
english_translation: A mother remains a mother even when her child behaves badly.
literal_translation: A mother is a mother even if the child is a bad child.
cultural_note: Marks the maternal bond as unconditional in a way few other relationships are treated. Often heard when a family is deciding how to handle a difficult child.

target_text: Nwaanyị bụ ụlọ
english_translation: Women are central to building and maintaining the family.
literal_translation: A woman is the home.
cultural_note: Ụlọ here means the household as an institution rather than the building. The proverb is used in marriage rites and in praise of a wife or mother.

target_text: Nwa bụ nke ọha
english_translation: The whole community shares responsibility for raising a child.
literal_translation: A child belongs to the community.
cultural_note: Underlies the practice of communal correction, in which any adult may guide or discipline any child, and the expectation that a village shares in a child's success.

target_text: Ihe okenye hụrụ n'ala nwata agaghị ahụ ya n'elu osisi
english_translation: Experience gives elders insight that youth may not possess.
literal_translation: What an elder sees sitting on the ground, a child cannot see from the top of a tree.
cultural_note: The classic defence of seniority in Igbo deliberation. Height, a proxy for advantage, is deliberately given to the child so that experience alone accounts for the difference.
